podcast.body: This top 10 hit, reaching number six in 1972, was Rick Nelson's last major success and was written in a "fit of pique." Despite its mellow sound, it functions as a diss record, expressing Nelson's anger at his audience's poor reception at a nostalgic multi-act concert at New York's Madison Square Garden in the fall of 1971. Nelson, performing as Rick Nelson, felt that the "hippie crowd" sat on their hands and even booed him, leading him to storm off stage and write the song, which contains coded references to other acts like Chuck Berry ("Johnny Be Good") and backstage attendees like John Lennon ("Yoko's Walrus") and George Harrison ("Mr. Hughes"). "It's a catchy song with very petty lyrics. And it was Rick Nelson's last big hit, reaching number 6 in 1972."

podcast.body: Written by Nelson after he was booed off stage at Madison Square Garden in October 1971 for performing country rock instead of his earlier rock and roll hits. The lyrics reflect on the audience's expectation for his 1950s image and music, and his decision to prioritize his own artistic path over pleasing everyone. The song includes lines about playing old songs, not looking the same, and the adage "you can't please everyone so you got to please yourself," as well as a reference to Johnny B. Goode. "So Nelson wrote about that night and he turned it into a song. Played them all the old songs. Thought that's why they came. No one heard the music. We didn't look the same."
